title: Agentic AI at a glance
intro: Each chapter in a few visual slides: the mental model, the distinctions the questions turn on, and the concepts to practise next.

chapters.hook: Decide who owns control flow, then design the system around failure.

slides.title: Who owns control flow?
slides.lede: The one distinction everything else hangs on. In a workflow, code decides the next step. In an agent, the model chooses actions and when to stop. Model count, retrieval and hardware do not change which one you have.

items.label: Prompt chain
items.sub: Fixed sequence, each output feeds the next

items.label: Routing
items.sub: Classify once, send to the right handler

items.label: Parallel fan-out
items.sub: Independent subtasks, merged at the end

items.label: Orchestrator–worker
items.sub: A coordinator picks who works next

items.label: Evaluator–optimizer
items.sub: Critique drives revision until criteria pass

items.label: ReAct loop
items.sub: Path unknown; adapts to every observation

points.h: Use the least autonomy that works
points.t: Every step you hand to the model is a step you can no longer guarantee.

points.h: Known order belongs in the graph
points.t: If the sequence is known in advance, encode it as a state machine rather than asking the model to remember it.

slides.title: The agent loop
slides.lede: An agent is a loop around a model: reason about the goal, call a tool, read the result, repeat. The engineering is in what bounds that loop and what survives when it breaks.

nodes.label: Goal + state
nodes.sub: What the task is, what is known

nodes.label: Act
nodes.sub: Tool call, executed by your code

visual.loop: repeat until a termination condition or the step budget is hit

points.t: A stop condition and a step budget. Without them, two agents can ping-pong a task until the limit.
Checkpoint graph state after every step, keyed by thread id, so a pod restart resumes instead of restarting.
Make the side-effecting node terminal and idempotent, so a retry cannot pay an invoice twice.

slides.title: Single or multi-agent?
slides.lede: More agents means more coordination, more tokens and more places to fail. Split only when the parts genuinely need different tools, context or permissions — or when there is real parallelism to win.

items.label: Single agent + tools
items.sub: The default. One context, one loop.

items.label: Supervisor
items.sub: A coordinator delegates to specialists and decides when done.

items.label: Hierarchical
items.sub: Supervisors of supervisors, for large tool sets.

items.label: Group chat
items.sub: Peers share a thread; needs speaker selection and a stop rule.

slides.takeaway: Not a reason to go multi-agent: a long prompt, or mirroring the org chart. A reason: tool-selection accuracy falling as tools are added — partition them behind sub-agents.

slides.title: Two protocols, two boundaries
slides.lede: Standard protocols replace one-off integrations. They answer different questions: what can this agent use, and which other agent can it hand work to?

cols.title: MCP
items: Servers expose tools, resources and prompts
One server, reusable by any compatible agent

cols.title: A2A
items: Capabilities advertised in an agent card
Neither side sees the other's internals

points.t: Inter-agent handoffs that parse inconsistently need a validated message schema, not a better prompt.

slides.title: Design for failure
slides.lede: Most architecture questions describe a symptom and ask for the structural fix. Learn the pairs.

rows: Model skips a required step or repeats a side effect
Encode the order in a graph; terminal, idempotent side-effect node
A flaky dependency aborts whole runs
Bounded retries, circuit breaker, a documented degraded path
Long job dies on pod restart
Durable checkpoint per step, keyed by thread id
Router or cascade: small model for simple intents
Add decomposition and synthesis, not just routing

slides.takeaway: Hard real-time paths do not contain LLM loops. A fast tier decides; the agentic tier investigates asynchronously.

chapters.hook: Tools, schemas, errors and tests: where agents actually break.

slides.title: Function calling: the model only proposes
slides.lede: The model never executes anything. It emits a structured request; your code validates, authorizes and runs it, then hands the result back as a message.

points.t: Validation and authorization happen between propose and execute, where the model cannot talk past them.
Arguments stream as fragments. Accumulate them and parse once the call is complete.

slides.title: Design tools the model can choose correctly
slides.lede: A tool's name, schema and description are prompt surface. Vague tools cause wrong selection, bad arguments and over-invocation.

cols.title: Hard to use
items: Description says what it is, not when to use it

cols.title: Easy to use
items: States what it returns, when to use it — and when not
Allowed values enumerated in the schema

slides.takeaway: Selection accuracy falls as the tool count grows. Past a few dozen, retrieve a candidate subset per turn or partition tools behind sub-agents.

slides.title: Structured output: the reliability ladder
slides.lede: Every rung is more reliable than the one before. Questions often offer a lower rung as a distractor when the stem calls for a guarantee.

items.label: “Respond only in JSON”
items.sub: No guarantee

items.label: Few-shot format examples
items.sub: Better, still probabilistic

items.label: Regex extraction or LLM repair
items.sub: Fixes failures after the fact

items.label: Schema validation + error back
items.sub: Catches all, costs a turn

items.label: Constrained decoding
items.sub: Malformed output is impossible

slides.title: Prompting an agent: what goes where
slides.lede: An agent's prompt is assembled every turn from parts with different jobs. Where each part sits decides how reliably the model uses it.

visual.top: start of context · stable, cacheable prefix
visual.bottom: end of context · most recent, most attended

layers.label: System prompt
layers.sub: Role, rules, tool-use policy, when to stop or ask

layers.label: Tool catalog
layers.sub: Names, schemas, descriptions — identical every turn

layers.label: Few-shot examples
layers.sub: Format and edge cases; the model copies them closely

layers.label: Critical constraints, re-asserted
layers.sub: Instructions far from the end get diluted in long runs

points.t: Low temperature for tool calls and extraction; several samples at non-zero temperature only when you will vote over them.
A clarifying question names the ambiguity, lists the options and says what each answer will do.

slides.title: Errors are prompt input
slides.lede: Whatever a tool returns on failure is what the model reasons over next. Make it actionable, make it loud, and make retries safe.

items.label: Actionable errors
items.text: Name the invalid field, the constraint and a valid example. Never a raw stack trace or a silent empty result.

items.label: Unknown tool name
items.text: Return an error listing the valid names. Never fuzzy-match to the nearest one.

items.label: Safe retries
items.text: Idempotency keys, or operations that are naturally idempotent — set-to-value, not increment-by.

items.label: Destructive tools
items.text: Dry run with affected counts, explicit confirmation, a server-side cap on blast radius.

items.label: Shared rate limits
items.text: A distributed token bucket or a queue. Per-process counters multiply the limit by replica count.

slides.title: Test in layers
slides.lede: Fast, deterministic tests at the bottom; slow, judged, sampled evaluation at the top. Each layer catches what the others cannot.

layers.label: Production
layers.sub: Sampled automated proxies plus a human-reviewed slice

layers.label: Integration
layers.sub: Recorded tool fixtures; trajectory and state-transition assertions

layers.label: Unit / CI
layers.sub: Stubbed model responses; exact tool calls and arguments; schema contracts

slides.takeaway: Temperature 0 is not reproducibility. Batching, kernels and model versions shift results — determinism comes from stubs and fixtures.

chapters.hook: Measure the right thing, trust the number only as far as it deserves, then pick the fix that matches the failure.

slides.title: Outcome is not enough
slides.lede: A correct final answer can hide a wasteful, risky or lucky path. Agent evaluation scores the trajectory too.

cols.title: Outcome evaluation
items: Blind to how the agent got there

cols.title: Trajectory evaluation
items: Catches the right answer in 11 calls instead of 3

points.t: Right tool, insufficient output: a tool or data gap. Malformed arguments: schema and prompting. Context lacks the answer: retrieval.

slides.title: The RAG triad
slides.lede: Three pairwise checks between question, retrieved context and answer. Whichever one fails tells you which stage is broken.

edges.label: Context relevance
edges.sub: Did retrieval fetch material about the question? Fails → fix retrieval.

edges.label: Groundedness
edges.sub: Is every claim supported by the context? Fails → the model is inventing.

edges.label: Answer relevance
edges.sub: Does the answer address what was asked? Fails → response targeting.

slides.takeaway: None of the triad needs a reference answer. Context recall does — it checks retrieved context against the reference's claims.

slides.title: LLM-as-judge, done properly
slides.lede: A model can grade at scale, but only after you have checked that its grades agree with people.

nodes.label: Anchored rubric
nodes.sub: What each score means, with examples

points.t: For open-ended comparison, ask which is better with randomized position, not for a 1–10 score.
Reusing the generator model and prompt as the judge brings self-preference bias.

slides.title: How far to trust the number
slides.lede: Most evaluation questions are really about whether a metric means what it seems to.

items.label: on 60 examples
items.text: Roughly two examples. Check run-to-run variance before believing it.

items.label: overall vs one task type
items.text: The aggregate hides a failing segment. Always disaggregate.

items.label: offline vs production
items.text: A stale eval set, overfitted. Mine production failures to refresh it.

items.label: right answer is in there
items.text: A selection problem: self-consistency, verification or reranking — not a bigger model.

items.label: aggregate score after quantizing
items.text: Benchmarks average across behaviours. Schema conformance or long-context recall can collapse underneath — re-test what the agent depends on.

items.label: for adversarial and routine traffic
items.text: Report the adversarial and high-consequence slices separately; they need different thresholds.

slides.title: Match the fix to the failure
slides.lede: Fine-tuning is rarely the first answer. The questions reward the cheapest intervention that addresses the actual cause.
slides.takeaway: After narrow fine-tuning, watch for catastrophic forgetting: mix in general replay data, lower the rank and learning rate — and re-evaluate the capabilities you depend on.

slides.title: Which benchmark measures what
slides.lede: Benchmark names come up as answer options. Know what each one actually tests — and which one is not what it is claimed to be.

head: Benchmark
Measures
rows: Function calling: selection, arguments, parallel calls, knowing when not to call
General assistant tasks needing tools and multi-step reasoning

slides.takeaway: CLASSic — Cost, Latency, Accuracy, Stability, Security — is Aisera's framework, not NVIDIA's. Some prep material gets this wrong.

chapters.hook: Where the milliseconds and the gigabytes go, and the technique that fixes each.

slides.title: Anatomy of a request
slides.lede: An LLM request has two phases with different bottlenecks. Prefill reads the whole prompt at once and is compute-bound. Decode emits one token at a time and is bound by memory bandwidth.

points.t: Time to first token grows with prompt length and queueing. Prefix caching and shorter context attack it.
Time per output token is set by memory bandwidth and batch size. Speculative decoding and quantization attack it.
Throughput that meets the latency SLO. Utilization can look excellent while every user waits.

slides.title: The KV cache is where memory goes
slides.lede: Every token in flight keeps its attention keys and values in GPU memory. At long context and high concurrency that cache outgrows the weights — and it is what runs out first.

visual.note: GPU memory, illustrative: a long-context deployment under load.

points.t: Allocates the cache in pages, ending fragmentation and over-reservation, and lets requests share a prefix.
The system prompt and tool catalog are identical every turn. Cache their prefill once.
Session affinity or KV-aware routing keeps a conversation on the replica that already holds its prefix.

slides.title: Serving techniques and what each fixes
slides.lede: Most deployment questions name a symptom. Pick the technique aimed at that bottleneck, not the one that sounds most advanced.

rows: Static batches idling until the longest sequence finishes
One huge prompt blocking short requests (head-of-line blocking)
Compute-bound prefill and bandwidth-bound decode fighting over one GPU
Weight memory and bandwidth; precision-critical behaviour must be re-tested
N fine-tuned variants without N full deployments

slides.title: Speculative decoding
slides.lede: Verifying several proposed tokens costs about one forward pass of the big model. So let a cheap drafter guess, and keep the guesses the target agrees with.

nodes.label: Draft
nodes.sub: Small model or extra heads propose k tokens

nodes.label: Verify
nodes.sub: Target model checks all k in one pass

nodes.label: Continue
nodes.sub: Output identical to the target alone

visual.loop: repeat from the first rejected token

points.t: Predictable output — boilerplate, structured formats, code — gains most. Highly variable text rejects most drafts.
If the cost is in a long prompt, it attacks the wrong phase. Multi-token prediction applies the same idea inside one model.

slides.title: Parallelism: fitting versus scaling
slides.lede: Three strategies split one model so it fits; one copies the whole model so you can serve more. Questions test which is which.

head: Strategy
Splits
Use
rows: Fit a large model at low latency — keep inside one NVLink domain

slides.takeaway: MoE sizing: compute like the active parameters, memory like the total. Every expert has to be resident.

slides.title: Running it on Kubernetes
slides.lede: GPU inference breaks several defaults that work for ordinary web services.

rows: Scale on queue depth, pending requests or GPU metrics
Scale to zero for bursty traffic
Warm baseline replicas plus fast scale-out; cold starts take minutes
Generous startup probe for weight loading; weights cached on the node
Include real tool and retrieval dependencies, or capacity is overstated
Reuse the engine on new GPUs
Rebuild: TensorRT-LLM engines are specific to model, precision and GPU

slides.title: Cost is a design decision
slides.lede: The big savings are architectural and made before launch, not found by tuning afterwards.

items.label: Cascade and route
items.text: A small model for easy intents, a large one for hard reasoning. Cost is usually dominated by easy traffic.

items.label: Cache
items.text: Prompt-prefix caching for repeated context; a semantic cache for repeated questions.

items.label: Context discipline
items.text: Every token of tool output and history is paid for again on every step of the loop.

items.label: Self-hosting
items.text: Buys data residency and version control. Cheaper only at high utilization.

chapters.hook: How agents reason, plan, remember and manage what they can see.

slides.title: Reasoning patterns
slides.lede: From one chain of thought to search with feedback. Each step right spends more compute to handle harder, less predictable problems.

items.label: Chain-of-Thought
items.sub: Intermediate steps before the answer

items.label: Self-consistency
items.sub: Several chains, majority answer

items.label: Least-to-most
items.sub: Ordered sub-problems, solved in turn

items.label: ReAct
items.sub: Thought, action, observation, interleaved

items.label: Tree of Thoughts
items.sub: Search with evaluation and backtracking

items.label: Reflexion
items.sub: Verbal self-feedback conditions the retry

points.h: A trace is not an explanation
points.t: Chain-of-thought is not a faithful account of the model's computation. A fluent chain can rationalize a wrong answer.
Reasoning models improve with more thinking tokens on hard tasks and gain nothing on easy ones. Tune per task class.

slides.title: How much to plan up front
slides.lede: Planning trades adaptability against cost. The right choice depends on how much the world can change between steps.

cols.title: ReAct
items: Can drift from the goal on long tasks

cols.title: Plan–Act–Replan
items: Plan only as far as is known

points.t: Triggered by an invalidated assumption, a failed step or new information — not a fixed cadence, and not every step.
Goal drift over long horizons is fixed by an explicit plan in durable state, not by a longer context.

slides.title: Reflexion: learning without weights
slides.lede: An agent can improve across attempts without any training. The learning lives in memory, as written feedback on what went wrong.

visual.loop: no weight updates at any point

points.t: Means no accessible attempt log — an episodic-memory gap, not a context-size problem.
A wrong inference stored as fact is retrieved and reinforced. Tag confidence, keep provenance, allow expiry.

slides.title: Kinds of memory
slides.lede: Borrowed from cognitive science, and useful because each kind needs a different store and a different write rule.

head: Memory
Holds
Example
rows: The current context, bounded by the window
What was tried, and what happened
Fixed at training — uncitable, no update path

slides.takeaway: Anything that must be current, citable or correctable belongs in retrieval, not in the weights. Tell the model to prefer provided context when the two conflict.

slides.title: Memory is decided at write time
slides.lede: A memory store is only as good as what gets written to it and how stale entries are retired.

items.label: Write policy
items.text: Store durable, future-relevant facts — not raw turns or transient task state.

items.label: Supersession
items.text: A new fact invalidates the old one it contradicts. Without a rule, stale advice resurfaces.

items.label: Retrieval scoring
items.text: Relevance alone surfaces stale memories. Weigh relevance, recency and importance.

items.label: System of record
items.text: Mutable state such as balances or order status is read live, not remembered.

slides.title: Managing the context window
slides.lede: Long runs outgrow any window. Good compaction is selective, not positional — it decides what survives by what it is, not where it sits.

cols.title: Summarize
items: Old tool outputs already acted on
Reasoning that led to settled decisions

cols.title: Keep verbatim
items: Exact identifiers — IDs, amounts, file paths

points.t: Models use the start and end of a long context more reliably than the middle. Put the best material at the edges.
Page detail out to external memory and retrieve it on demand, rather than carrying everything in the window.

chapters.hook: Getting the right, current, permitted evidence in front of the model — and knowing which layer failed when you don't.

slides.title: The retrieval pipeline
slides.lede: Half the pipeline runs at ingest time, half at query time. Most retrieval failures trace back to one specific stage.

slides.title: Diagnose by symptom
slides.lede: Name the failing layer before choosing a fix. Tuning the generator cannot fix a retrieval problem.

head: Symptom
Layer
Fix
rows: Exact codes and SKUs not found
Add BM25 and fuse — hybrid search
Dedupe at ingest; MMR for diversity

slides.title: Embeddings and indexes
slides.lede: Retrieve broad and cheap, then rank narrow and precise. Two encoder types do those two jobs.

cols.title: Bi-encoder
items: Documents embedded once, ahead of time

points.t: HNSW: high recall and low latency, large memory. IVF-PQ: compressed and smaller, some recall loss — for sets that outgrow RAM.
Post-filtering discards results after retrieval, so a selective filter silently returns almost nothing.
A new embedding model invalidates the whole index. Generators swap freely.

slides.title: Beyond plain top-k
slides.lede: RAG variants each patch a specific weakness of retrieve-once-and-generate.

items.label: HyDE
items.text: Embed a hypothetical answer instead of the raw question, so the query looks like the documents.

items.label: Self-RAG
items.text: Decide whether to retrieve at all; critique and grade what comes back.

items.label: Corrective RAG
items.text: Grade the retrieved documents; rewrite the query or fall back when they are poor.

items.label: RAPTOR
items.text: Recursively cluster and summarize into a tree; serve detail or synthesis by question scope.

items.label: GraphRAG
items.text: Extract entities and relations so multi-hop links can be traversed.

slides.title: Not everything is similarity search
slides.lede: Some data loses its meaning when flattened into text chunks, and some questions are computations, not lookups.

rows: Layout-aware extraction: OCR, table structure, figure captions
A query tool over a table — embeddings cannot compute a sum
A time-series store behind range and aggregate query tools
Extracted as untrusted data, fenced like any retrieved content

slides.title: Current, permitted, citable
slides.lede: Relevance is not enough. Evidence also has to be the current version, allowed for this user, and traceable to its source.

items.label: Freshness
items.text: Effective-date metadata, query-time filters, tombstones for superseded versions; content hashes for incremental updates.

items.label: Permissions
items.text: Tenant and per-user access enforced inside the query, server-side, before anything reaches the prompt.

items.label: PII
items.text: Redact or tokenize at ingestion. If it is never embedded, it cannot be retrieved or leaked.

items.label: Citations
items.text: Stable chunk IDs carried into the prompt, cited per claim, and checked after generation.

chapters.hook: Which NVIDIA component does what — and the pairs that are easy to confuse.

slides.title: The model lifecycle, product by product
slides.lede: NeMo splits the model lifecycle into services. Know which stage each one owns.
slides.takeaway: Curator vs Customizer vs Evaluator: data in, weights changed, quality measured. RL post-training in tool-using environments is NeMo Gym with NeMo RL.

slides.title: The serving stack
slides.lede: Four serving products that sound alike and sit at different levels.

head: Component
What it is
Not to be confused with
rows: A packaged, versioned microservice for one model, with a standard API
Triton — a NIM may use Triton or TensorRT-LLM inside
Builds and runs the optimized inference engine
NIM, which wraps an engine into a deployable container
A general multi-model, multi-framework server, with ensembles
A distributed serving framework: disaggregates prefill from decode and routes by KV cache
A per-GPU engine optimization — it works across nodes and GPUs

slides.title: Around the agent
slides.lede: The rest of the product map, by the job you need done.

rows: Extract, embed and rerank documents for RAG
GPU-accelerate vector index build and search
Compose and profile agents across frameworks
Start from a working reference workflow
Try models with no GPU, then self-host the winner

slides.takeaway: NeMo Retriever is not a vector database. It provides the extraction, embedding and reranking services; the index itself is Milvus, Elasticsearch, pgvector or similar.

slides.title: Choosing hardware
slides.lede: Most hardware questions come down to memory: how much there is, and how fast GPUs share it.

items.label: 80 GB → 141 GB
items.text: Same Hopper compute. More HBM and bandwidth means a bigger KV cache: more concurrency, longer context per GPU.

items.label: GPU-to-GPU interconnect
items.text: Tensor parallelism all-reduces every layer, so it stays inside one NVLink domain.

items.label: one GPU, isolated slices
items.text: Co-host small models — embedder, reranker, guardrail — with guaranteed quality of service.

items.label: GB200
items.text: Adds FP4 arithmetic; Grace-based superchips couple a CPU tightly to the GPU.

slides.title: Nemotron
slides.lede: NVIDIA's open-weight model family, and the architecture choices behind it.

items.label: one family
items.text: A cascade across sizes shares prompting behaviour and toolchain.

items.label: hybrid architecture
items.text: Mamba layers scale linearly with length; attention layers keep precise recall.

items.label: a fraction of parameters active
items.text: Computes like a small model; memory is still sized by total parameters.

items.label: tokens of native context
items.text: Trained with NVFP4 and multi-token prediction; RL post-trained with NeMo Gym.

items.label: open weights
items.text: Commercial use under its terms — not a permissive OSI licence.

slides.title: Many variants, one base model
slides.lede: Fine-tuned variants that differ by a sliver of their parameters should not each cost a full deployment.

cols.title: Full deployment each
items: Forty variants, forty copies of the base weights

cols.title: Multi-LoRA
items: Variants trained as small LoRA adapters
The adapter is picked per request

slides.takeaway: Train the adapters with NeMo Customizer; serve them with NIM's multi-LoRA support. MIG and Curator are distractors here.

chapters.hook: Seeing what the agent did, noticing when it degrades, and changing it without breaking it.

slides.title: A trace is a tree, not a log
slides.lede: One root span per task, with a child span for every model call, retrieval and tool call. Flat logs lose which step caused which.

points.t: OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions name spans and attributes — model, tokens, latency, status — so traces port across vendors.
They hold prompts and tool arguments. Redact at capture, restrict access, set retention.

slides.title: SLIs for agents
slides.lede: An HTTP 200 says nothing about whether the task got done. Agent indicators are measured per task, across the whole trajectory.

head: Indicator
Agentic version
rows: Task success against a defined acceptance criterion
p95 end-to-end task completion, across every step
Cost per completed task, prompt and completion tokens split
Steps and tool calls per task; how often runs hit the step limit

slides.takeaway: Leading indicators: step-limit terminations and tool-error or retry rates rise before users complain.

slides.title: Drift: the stack is frozen, the world isn't
slides.lede: Quality can fall with no deploy at all. The traffic and the corpus moved, even though the code didn't.

items.label: Slow decline, no change
items.text: With a frozen stack, that is drift. Compare today's inputs and retrievals against the eval set's.

items.label: Pin model versions
items.text: A floating “latest” alias changes behaviour with no change on your side.

items.label: Scheduled re-evaluation
items.text: Re-run the eval suite on a cadence and on fresh production samples, not only at release.

items.label: Close the loop
items.text: Production failures become eval cases and training data — the data flywheel.

slides.title: Responding to an incident
slides.lede: A sharp change in behaviour has a time boundary. Find it and find what changed there, before touching anything.

nodes.label: Correlate
nodes.sub: Deploys, prompt edits, model or dependency changes

nodes.label: Diff traces
nodes.sub: Same task type, either side of it

nodes.label: Lock it in
nodes.sub: Add the case to the regression suite

points.t: Rolling back without a diagnosis can remove the wrong change and hide the real one.
Error on missing or unexpected fields at tool boundaries. Silent nulls make agents confidently wrong.

slides.title: Version everything that shapes behaviour
slides.lede: An agent's behaviour is the joint product of six things. To reproduce or audit a past decision you need all of them.
slides.takeaway: An audit record needs the full trajectory on top: inputs, retrieved sources with versions, every tool call and result, and any human approvals.

slides.title: Releasing a change
slides.lede: Each stage exposes the change to more reality at more risk, and each has a comparison against control.

nodes.label: Canary
nodes.sub: Small share of the same traffic mix

points.t: Task success, tool-error rate, cost per task and latency against control — held long enough to see real variety.

chapters.hook: Assume the model can be talked into anything, and bound what it can do anyway.

slides.title: Where the rails sit
slides.lede: Guardrails intercept at five points in a request. Each sees different content and stops different things.
slides.takeaway: Output filtering protects what the user sees, not what the system did. An agent that already sent the money has caused the harm — consequential actions need authorization before execution.

slides.title: Injection: content is data
slides.lede: An agent reads text from places attackers can write to. Anything it reads can contain instructions — only the channel differs.

cols.title: Direct
items: Assume bypass; bound consequences at the tool layer

cols.title: Indirect
items: Documents, web pages, email, text in images
Fence and label as untrusted data
Retrieval rails; never promote it into the system prompt

cols.title: Supply chain
items: Poisoned tool descriptions or MCP servers
Verify provenance; alert on metadata changes

slides.title: Bound the blast radius
slides.lede: Detection always misses something. The controls that hold are the ones enforced outside the model.

rows: Least-privilege credentials; approval enforced by the orchestrator for irreversible actions
Act with the requesting user's authority, not the agent's service account
Tools scoped to allowlists, proxied egress, no ambient credentials
A sandbox: no credentials, no network, minimal mounts, hard resource limits
Moderated contributions, provenance tracking, filtering at the retrieval rail

slides.title: The EU AI Act's risk tiers
slides.lede: Obligations scale with the risk of the use case, not the capability of the model.

items.label: Minimal risk
items.sub: Most applications; voluntary codes

items.label: Limited risk
items.sub: Transparency: say it is an AI

items.label: High risk
items.sub: e.g. recruitment screening; strict duties

items.label: Prohibited
items.sub: Practices banned outright

points.t: People must be told they are dealing with an AI unless it is obvious — whatever the risk tier.
NIST AI RMF is Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — not the Cybersecurity Framework's Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond. Also OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS.

slides.title: Privacy and fairness
slides.lede: Both fail quietly: personal data that is reachable when it shouldn't be, and disparate impact hidden inside a good average.

cols.title: Privacy
items: Minimize at ingestion — redact PII before embedding
Self-hosting keeps prompts inside your boundary
Erasure: index entries delete cleanly; tuned weights need retraining
Trace stores are personal data too

cols.title: Fairness
items: Counterfactual tests that vary only group-linked attributes
Removing a field does not remove its proxies
The retrieval path can carry bias too

chapters.hook: Human oversight that actually controls something, rather than signing off on it.

slides.title: In, on or out of the loop
slides.lede: How much a human is involved should follow the stakes of the action, not habit.

items.label: Human in the loop
items.sub: Approves before anything happens. Irreversible or high-consequence actions.

items.label: Human on the loop
items.sub: Monitors and can intervene. High-volume, reversible actions.

items.label: Human out of the loop
items.sub: Fully autonomous. Only with measured reliability on that action.

slides.takeaway: Autonomy is set by potential harm × irreversibility, weighed against measured reliability on that specific action — not by frequency, duration, or whether the API is internal.

slides.title: Autonomy is earned per action
slides.lede: Reliability measured on one kind of case says nothing about another. Widen autonomy one measured scope at a time.

nodes.label: Shadow
nodes.sub: Agent proposes, humans decide; measure agreement

nodes.label: Approve each
nodes.sub: Human in the loop on every action

nodes.label: Approve by exception
nodes.sub: Human on the loop; sampled audit

points.h: Scope is part of the evidence
points.t: Accuracy on sub-$50 refunds does not transfer to $500 ones. Out-of-scope cases route back to a lower-autonomy path.

slides.title: Oversight theatre
slides.lede: Rubber-stamping is the default failure of human review. Forty pending items at four seconds each is accountability without control.

cols.title: Rubber stamp
items: Rejecting takes more effort than approving

cols.title: Real review
items: States exactly what approval will do, and whether it can be undone
Rejecting is as cheap as approving

slides.title: Escalate on signals you can verify
slides.lede: A model's own confidence is poorly calibrated. Escalation triggers should be facts the system can check.

cols.title: Verifiable
items: The request matches an out-of-scope rule

slides.title: Make it recoverable
slides.lede: Logging records harm; recoverability limits it. Every destructive action gets guard rails before it runs and an undo path after.

nodes.label: Dry run
nodes.sub: Report what would be affected, and how much

nodes.label: Cap
nodes.sub: A server-side limit on blast radius

slides.title: Handoffs and feedback
slides.lede: When the agent passes work to a person, pass understanding, not a transcript. When the person corrects it, treat that as data.

cols.title: Raw transcript
items: Repeats work the agent already did

points.h: Feedback with a reason and a trace
points.t: A thumbs-down with a reason category and a trace ID points to the failing step. Fix prompts, tools or retrieval first; tune last.
Time for the human to decide, and how often they must re-gather context the agent already had.

slides.title: What users are owed
slides.lede: Transparency means the things that affect a user's decisions and rights — not the system's internals.

items.label: It's an AI
items.text: Disclosed unless obvious. Required regardless of risk tier.

items.label: Where claims come from
items.text: Sources the user can check, and what the agent could not verify.

items.label: A route to a human
items.text: A clear way out when the agent is not the right answer.

slides.takeaway: Not owed, and usually a distractor: parameter counts, the system prompt, or narrated chain-of-thought presented as an explanation.
